js_003: Who was the British historian who wrote What Is History?
js_005: Arnold Toynbee, who wrote A Study of History
js_006: Karl Popper, of The Open Society and Its Enemies
js_007: Alexis de Tocqueville, of The Old Regime and the Revolution
js_008: What Is History? was published in 1961 by E. H. Carr (1892–1982), a British historian and former diplomat. Having spent his life studying Soviet history, he turned to question the discipline of history itself.
js_010: What was this book originally based on?
js_011: A 1961 lecture series at the University of Cambridge
js_012: A graduate seminar held at Oxford University
js_013: A history lecture series broadcast on BBC Radio
js_014: A collection of history columns from a London newspaper
js_015: Six lectures delivered as the George Macaulay Trevelyan Lectures at Cambridge from January to March 1961 became this book almost word for word. The lecture-hall tone still lives in every sentence.
js_017: Which is Carr’s most famous definition of history?
js_018: An unending dialogue between the present and the past
js_019: An accurate restoration of records left by a bygone age
js_020: A collection of stories about great men’s deeds
js_021: The work of extracting laws from recurring events
js_022: Carr’s answer was a constant interaction between the historian and the facts, an unending dialogue between the present and the past. That single line became the motto for a century of history students.
js_024: What did Carr compare historical facts to?
js_025: Fish swimming in a vast ocean
js_026: Fish laid neatly on a fishmonger’s slab
js_028: Entries anyone can look up in a dictionary
js_029: Facts, Carr says, are not fish on a fishmonger’s slab but fish swimming in a vast ocean. What gets caught depends on which sea the historian fishes in and what tackle they use.
js_031: What is Carr’s answer to the common belief that facts speak for themselves?
js_032: Facts speak only when the historian calls on them
js_033: Facts always reveal the truth on their own
js_034: More facts means interpretation becomes unnecessary
js_035: A fact is complete the moment it’s recorded
js_036: Carr flatly states that the idea of facts speaking for themselves is simply not true. It’s always the historian who decides which facts get a voice, and in what order and context.
js_038: Whose slogan for 19th-century positivist history did Carr criticize?
js_039: ‘As it actually happened’ — Leopold von Ranke
js_043: German historian Ranke held that the historian’s task was to show things as they actually happened. Carr argues this attitude hardened into a cult of worshipping facts.
js_044: Which is Carr’s major historical work, nearly 30 years in the making?
js_045: A History of Soviet Russia, in 14 volumes
js_046: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, in six volumes
js_048: The Making of the English Working Class, in two volumes
js_049: From 1950 to 1978, Carr published the 14-volume A History of Soviet Russia. That massive work, covering only the twelve years after the revolution (1917–1929), was his life’s main project — this book was a lecture series he wrote in between.
js_050: What other book by Carr is considered a classic of international relations?
js_053: The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers
js_055: Published in 1939, The Twenty Years’ Crisis reads the interwar international order as a clash between idealism and realism. Carr was a Foreign Office official before he was a historian.
js_057: How many lectures make up this book?
js_062: There are six lectures in all, running: The Historian and His Facts → Society and the Individual → History, Science, and Morality → Causation → Progress → The Widening Horizon.
js_063: What is the title of the first lecture?
js_065: Sources and How to Read Them
js_066: Questions to Ask of the Past
js_068: In Lecture One, The Historian and His Facts, Carr lays out the relationship between fact and interpretation. This first lecture is the book’s backbone — the other five simply expand on it.
js_084: Carr spent over twenty years working as a diplomat in the British Foreign Office. That someone who’d handled real international politics went on to question the very foundations of history gives the book its weight.
js_085: The Trevelyan Lectures are public talks Cambridge invites distinguished historians to give. Because they were spoken aloud to a live audience, the sentences stay short and the pushback still feels alive.
js_086: The original order is present-and-past, in that sequence. It’s often flipped and quoted as past-and-present, but what Carr placed first was always the present.
js_087: Which sea you fish in, and with what tackle, ultimately depends on which fish you want to catch. That’s why Carr states flatly that history is, in the end, interpretation.
js_088: Carr sees the cult of facts as a legacy of 19th-century British empiricism. The belief that history writes itself once enough facts are gathered is the first thing he tears down.
js_089: Ranke’s slogan was originally a modest call to set moral judgment aside. But Carr’s diagnosis is that later generations hardened it into the belief that simply gathering facts was enough.
js_090: This massive work stopped after covering just the first twelve years of the revolution. Carr had meant to write through 1945 but ran out of time; a condensed version, The Russian Revolution: From Lenin to Stalin, was published separately.
js_091: The Twenty Years’ Crisis is regarded as the starting point of realism in international relations. Carr is a rare figure who left his mark on both history and international relations theory.
js_092: The six lectures move through fact, agency, science, causation, progress, and outlook in turn. Follow the order of the lectures and you get a ready-made map of the philosophy of history.
js_093: The conclusion of Lecture One is the conclusion of the whole book. The remaining lectures simply widen the historian’s position across the layers of society, science, causation, and progress.
js_106: ↻ This question will come back later
js_108: A fact of the past and a historical fact are not the same. A fact becomes history only once historians select and cite it.
js_110: Facts aren’t fish on a slab — they’re fish swimming in a vast ocean. What gets caught depends on the angler.
js_112: A constant interaction between historian and fact. Questions from the present call out to the past, and the past reflects back on the present.
js_114: Before you open the book, read the historian; before you know the historian, know their society. Carr’s method is a triple reading.
js_116: The historian, too, is a product of their age. So history is also a dialogue not between individuals, but between societies.
js_118: There are always multiple causes. The historian’s job is to judge which of them carries the most weight.
js_120: Not a straight line that runs on its own, but a process of handing down and building on what earlier generations gained.
js_122: Is it dangerous relativism if facts shift depending on the historian? A classic clash at the heart of studying history.
js_124: In 1896, Lord Acton was confident that an ultimate history would one day be possible.
js_125: Sixty years later, George Clark wrote that such a history was impossible.
js_126: Facts, Carr says, aren’t fish on a slab — they’re fish swimming in the sea.
js_127: Facts don’t speak for themselves; they only speak when the historian calls on them.
js_128: Like the 1850 death of a street vendor, an uncited fact isn’t history yet.
js_129: Conclusion — history is an unending dialogue between the present and the past.
js_131: The historian isn’t a lone individual standing in a vacuum, but a product of society.
js_132: Read the historian before the book, Carr advises, and the society before the historian.
js_133: Great figures are representatives and amplifiers of forces their era pushed forward.
js_134: The axis is the interplay of individuals shaping society and society shaping individuals.
js_135: So history becomes a dialogue not between individuals, but between societies.
js_138: Carr argues history, too, generalizes, teaches, and makes conditional predictions like a science.
js_139: Even natural science’s laws are really hypotheses, so there’s no reason to hold history to a stricter standard.
js_140: Historical generalizations aren’t conclusions — they’re tools that guide the next inquiry.
js_141: He draws a firm line: moral judgment should never become a trial that condemns individuals.
js_142: Instead, judgment should fall on institutions and events — like slavery or a specific policy.
js_143: This positions the historian as a social evaluator, not a personal judge.
js_146: It opens with the line that the historian is someone who never stops asking why.
js_147: Causes are always plural, and the historian’s job is to build a hierarchy among them.
js_148: The example of Robinson, who died in an accident while out buying cigarettes, appears here.
js_149: Only causes that generalize — like drunk driving or faulty brakes — count as historical causes.
js_150: Chance events like Cleopatra’s nose exist, but they don’t lead anywhere as a lesson.
js_151: He adds the sharp observation that theories of chance usually come from the losing side.
js_153: He insists history has direction, but that direction isn’t an automatic straight line.
js_154: Progress is the process by which each generation inherits and builds on what the last one gained.
js_155: Unlike biological evolution passed on through genes, historical progress runs on learning and transmission.
js_156: That means setbacks are always possible — progress is no guaranteed promise.
js_157: Without a sense of direction toward the future, the historian can’t make sense of the past.
js_159: He sees the agents of history expanding from a small elite to a far wider range of people.
js_160: He reads the emergence of newly independent nations as the horizon widening.
js_161: He calls the expanding reach of reason the real revolution of the 20th century.
js_162: He pushes back directly against the pessimism and skepticism of his contemporaries in British intellectual life.
js_163: Even in his unfinished preface to the second edition, he stood firmly on the side of reason and progress to the end.
js_164: A confidence that collapsed in 60 years
js_165: In 1896, Lord Acton declared in the preface to the Cambridge Modern History that once all the sources were gathered, an ultimate history — with nothing left to revise — could one day be written. In 1957, George Clark, writing a new preface for the same project, stated that such a history was impossible.
js_166: Two prefaces for the same scholarly project reveal two eras’ entire worldviews. How might the certainties we take for granted today read sixty years from now?
js_168: In 1850, a gingerbread vendor at a market in Stalybridge was kicked to death by an angry crowd. It undeniably happened, but for a long time no history book mentioned it — until Carr brought it up in a lecture, and only then did people start talking about it.
js_169: Someone else entirely decides what becomes history. What facts in our society today still haven’t been cited by anyone?
js_171: Robinson stepped out to buy cigarettes and was killed on a blind curve by a car with faulty brakes, driven by a drunk man named Jones. Running out of cigarettes was clearly a cause too, but Carr says no policy can be built from that one.
js_172: The standard for choosing a cause ultimately comes down to what can actually be changed. When I name something as the cause of an event, does it really meet that standard?
js_173: Who chose what I believe to be fact?
js_174: Carr said facts don’t speak for themselves. Trace back the single news headline you were sure of today — what editing and selection did it pass through before reaching you?
js_175: As a product of which era and society am I looking at the past?
js_176: The claim that historians are products of their own society applies to us too. Name three things in your environment that set the defaults for your judgment.
js_177: Can I live facing tomorrow without believing in progress?
js_178: Carr’s progress isn’t a guarantee — it’s a handoff. Think of what you’d like to pass on to the next person.
